say: This is The Change Sentinel. It watches Nuh district in Haryana in free Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, finds new stone quarries, and hands officers a ranked list of case files, with the evidence attached.

Mining in the Aravalli hills of Nuh has been suspended by the Supreme Court since 2009, yet new pits keep appearing. Nobody compares images month after month across eighteen hundred square kilometres, and naive change detection drowns in clouds, monsoon green-up and harvests.

So we chose one change class: new open-cast quarries. Unauthorised can be decided, because mining in these hills is suspended. And the signal survives the seasons. A field is bare for a few months. A working quarry is bare rock in nearly every clear view, all year. A pixel is flagged when it is bare in at least three quarters of this year's clear views, far more often than last year, and its peak greenness has dropped.

The pipeline has eight steps. It loads the district boundary, searches Sentinel-2 scenes in the Earth Search catalogue, streams one date at a time into yearly statistics, adds land cover and slope, detects sites, assigns the village, tehsil and district, ranks them, and writes the case files.

Clouds and seasons cancel out by design. Each pixel is summarised over a full twelve months, so every season appears on both sides of the comparison. This chart compares a site with a ring around it. The monsoon moves both lines, but the quarry pulls the site down, and keeps it there.

Everything runs from one command, on a laptop. Imagery streams straight from public cloud-optimised files. The yearly composites are cached, so trying new thresholds or rankings does not download them again.

The output is a ranked list. Cases are grouped into Inspect, Review and Low, then ordered by confidence times area. Every row shows the village, the area with an uncertainty range, the confidence, and the window in which the change happened.

Each case file has a same-season before and after pair with an identical colour stretch, the monthly greenness chart, plain-language reasons for its rank, the jurisdiction from village to state, a field checklist, and an evidence trail with scene IDs and image hashes.

On a two hundred and eleven square kilometre test area, it read sixty-eight image dates and flagged nine sites. Five are worth sending someone to: a quarry expansion in Ghata Shamasabad, and four in an active cluster just across the Rajasthan border, marked for the neighbouring administration. Four on farmland are kept, but ranked last.

Compute discipline is part of the design. Each image block is downloaded once, only the three clearest dates per month are used, and the yearly stacks are stored as single bytes. The whole district needs about one and a half gigabytes of memory.

It is a lead, not proof. Confidence is not calibrated yet, the monsoon months need radar, and fallow fields can still look like quarries. Next, we label a hundred sites, add Sentinel-1 radar, and run the whole district every month.
Free data, open source, one command. The Change Sentinel: case files, not curiosities.
